chapter.name: New Beginnings: Cities and States
chapter.blurb: The Second Urbanisation, janapadas and mahajanapadas, governance, iron and coins, the varna-jati system and trade routes.

scope_in.item: Trade routes and cities beyond the Ganga plains

concepts.name: From the First to the Second Urbanisation
concepts.description: The end of Harappan cities, a millennium without urban life, and the new urbanisation of the Ganga plains and the sources that show it.
concepts.idea: After the Harappan cities faded, a second phase of urbanisation began in the 1st millennium BCE.
concepts.rule: The Harappan (First Urbanisation) civilisation disintegrated in the early 2nd millennium BCE and urban life was largely absent for about a thousand years. In the 1st millennium BCE a new phase, the Second Urbanisation, began in the Ganga plains, parts of the Indus basin and neighbouring regions. We know this from archaeological excavations and from ancient literature: late Vedic, Buddhist and Jain texts refer to the new urban centres.
concepts.example: The Harappan urban order had structures, markets, specialised occupations, writing, sanitation and an administration.

questions.q: The Harappan civilisation is called India's First ____.
questions.a: Urbanisation

questions.q: The Second Urbanisation began in the
questions.a: 1st millennium BCE

questions.q: Which region saw the new phase of urbanisation?
questions.a: the Ganga plains

questions.q: For about how long was urban life largely absent after the Harappan cities?
questions.a: a whole millennium

questions.q: Why did people in some Harappan cities return to village life?
questions.a: The components of the urban order had disappeared
o: The components of the urban order had disappeared

questions.q: Digging at ancient sites is called ____ excavation.
questions.a: archaeological

questions.q: How do we know about the Second Urbanisation?
questions.a: Archaeological excavations and ancient literature

questions.q: Which is NOT part of the Harappan urban order?
questions.a: Iron weapons in large armies

questions.q: List two features of the Harappan urban order that had disappeared by the early 2nd millennium BCE.
questions.a: For example elaborate structures, busy markets, specialised occupations, the writing system, the sanitation system and an administration.

questions.q: Buddhist and Jain texts describing towns are which type of source?
questions.a: literary

questions.q: Remains of city walls found by digging are which type of source?
questions.a: archaeological

questions.q: A historian finds a mound with brick walls and reads a text describing a city. Explain how both sources help her.
questions.a: The excavation confirms the city existed and shows its structures, while the text tells about its life and importance.

questions.q: Why is the Second Urbanisation said to continue even today?
questions.a: Cities that began in that period, many of them 2,500 years old, are still living cities and urban growth has continued.

questions.q: A student says India's cities began only 200 years ago. Which fact corrects this?
questions.a: Ancient capitals from the Second Urbanisation are still living cities
o: Ancient capitals from the Second Urbanisation are still living cities
Harappan cities were the only ones
There were no cities before railways

questions.q: Compare the First and Second Urbanisation in two ways.
questions.a: The First was the Harappan civilisation in the Indus region with copper and bronze and a script, while the Second began in the Ganga plains with iron and states called mahajanapadas.

questions.q: Why did the chapter say some regions had 'important regional cultures' between the two phases?
questions.a: Life continued in villages and regions even without large cities
o: Life continued in villages and regions even without large cities
The sea had covered the land

questions.q: Explain why urban life could not continue when the Harappan components disappeared.
questions.a: Cities need structures, markets, specialised workers, an administration and a state; when these were gone, people had to live in rural ways.

questions.q: Why are both archaeological and literary sources needed for history?
questions.a: Archaeology gives physical evidence of cities, while literature describes people, ideas and events that objects cannot show; together they give a fuller picture.

questions.q: Which source do you think is more reliable for ancient cities, excavation or literature? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned answer such as excavation gives direct evidence, while literature may be biased; but both are useful. Any balanced justification is accepted.

questions.q: Draw a timeline showing the Harappan civilisation, the gap and the Second Urbanisation with approximate dates.
questions.a: A timeline with the Harappan phase before about 1900 BCE, a gap of about a thousand years, and the Second Urbanisation from the 1st millennium BCE.

concepts.name: Janapadas and mahajanapadas
concepts.description: Clans and janapadas, the sixteen mahajanapadas, their capitals and why they clustered in the Ganga plains.
concepts.idea: Clans settled in janapadas which merged into sixteen large states called mahajanapadas.
concepts.rule: Towards the end of the 2nd millennium BCE clans became associated with a territory, a janapada, led by a raja. Janapada means where the people (jana) have set foot (pada). By the 8th or 7th centuries BCE some merged into mahajanapadas; the usual list has 16, from Gandhara in the northwest to Anga in the east and Ashmaka near the Godavari. The most powerful were Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti. Most were clustered in the fertile Ganga plains. Capitals were fortified cities with a moat.
concepts.example: The capital of Magadha was Rajagriha, in modern Bihar.

questions.q: Janapada means where the people have set ____.
questions.a: foot

questions.q: How many mahajanapadas are in the more frequent list?
Which was among the most powerful mahajanapadas?
questions.a: Magadha

questions.q: The capital of Kosala was
questions.a: Shravasti

questions.q: A janapada was
questions.a: a territory associated with a clan led by a raja
o: a territory associated with a clan led by a raja

questions.q: A deep, wide water-filled ditch around a fort is called a ____.
questions.a: moat

questions.q: Why were many mahajanapadas in the Ganga plains?
questions.a: Fertile land, iron ore nearby and new trade networks
o: Fertile land, iron ore nearby and new trade networks

questions.q: How did mahajanapadas arise from janapadas?
questions.a: Some early states merged into bigger units
o: Some early states merged into bigger units

questions.q: Explain what a janapada was and how its name shows this.
questions.a: It was a territory where a clan had settled under a raja; the word comes from jana, people, and pada, foot, meaning where people have set foot.

questions.q: Which mahajanapada lay in part of today's Bihar?
questions.a: Magadha

questions.q: Ujjayini was the capital of
questions.a: Avanti

questions.q: Name the capitals of Magadha, Vatsa and Avanti.
questions.a: Rajagriha for Magadha, Kaushambi for Vatsa and Ujjayini for Avanti.

questions.q: Why did capitals have a moat and narrow gateways?
questions.a: The moat and fortifications defended the city, and narrow gateways let guards control the movement of people and goods.

questions.q: Which fact shows how old India's cities are?
questions.a: Many ancient capitals are still cities about 2,500 years old
o: Many ancient capitals are still cities about 2,500 years old
Cities have only existed a century

questions.q: Suggest three reasons why the Ganga plains supported many mahajanapadas.
questions.a: Fertile land helped agriculture, iron ore in nearby mountains gave tools, and new trade networks connected the states.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say the borders on the map are 'approximate'?
questions.a: Ancient borders are not known exactly
o: Ancient borders are not known exactly

questions.q: Compare a janapada and a mahajanapada.
questions.a: A janapada was a smaller territory of a clan under a raja, while a mahajanapada was a bigger state formed by merging early states.

questions.q: Explain how trade helped janapadas grow into mahajanapadas.
questions.a: Trade connected the janapadas, increased wealth and links, and helped some merge into bigger states.

questions.q: 'Ancient capitals were small villages.' Do you agree? Justify with facts.
questions.a: No. Most were large, well-fortified cities with moats and gateways, and many still exist as cities.

questions.q: Make a table of five mahajanapadas with their capital and a modern state.
questions.a: A table such as Magadha - Rajagriha - Bihar, Kosala - Shravasti - Uttar Pradesh, Vatsa - Kaushambi - Uttar Pradesh, Avanti - Ujjayini - Madhya Pradesh, and one more.

concepts.name: Governance in the mahajanapadas: monarchies and republics
concepts.description: The role of the raja and assemblies, hereditary monarchies, and the ganas or sanghas of Vajji and Malla.
concepts.idea: Most mahajanapadas were monarchies with assemblies, while Vajji and Malla were early republics.
concepts.rule: Each janapada had an assembly, sabha or samiti, and a raja was expected to take advice from it and from ministers; an incompetent ruler could be removed according to some texts. In monarchies such as Magadha, Kosala and Avanti the raja was the ultimate authority and his position was hereditary. The raja collected taxes, kept order, built fortifications and kept an army. Vajji and Malla, called ganas or sanghas, gave the assembly more power; it decided by discussion and vote, even choosing the raja. Scholars call them early republics.
concepts.example: Vajji and its neighbour Malla are examples of ganas or sanghas.

questions.q: An assembly or council in a janapada was called a sabha or ____.
questions.a: samiti

questions.q: Which two mahajanapadas were ganas or sanghas?
questions.a: Vajji and Malla

questions.q: In a monarchy the raja's position was usually
questions.a: hereditary

questions.q: Another name for the early republics was
questions.a: ganas or sanghas

questions.q: What was the raja expected to do with the assemblies?
questions.a: Take their advice

questions.q: Vajji and Malla gave more power to the ____.
questions.a: assembly

questions.q: How were important decisions taken in the ganas?
questions.a: Through discussion and, if needed, voting
o: Through discussion and, if needed, voting

questions.q: Why are ganas called early republics?
questions.a: Assembly members selected the ruler and took major decisions
o: Assembly members selected the ruler and took major decisions
They had a king by birth

questions.q: List two duties of a raja in a mahajanapada.
questions.a: He collected taxes and maintained law and order, built fortifications and maintained an army.

questions.q: A state where the raja is the son of the previous raja and the ultimate authority is a
questions.a: monarchy

questions.q: In which kind of state could the assembly choose the ruler?
questions.a: a gana or sangha

questions.q: Magadha, Kosala and Avanti were monarchies. Vajji was not. State the main difference.
questions.a: In the monarchies the raja was the ultimate authority with a hereditary post, but in Vajji the assembly decided and selected the ruler.

questions.q: Why can't we be sure that a ruler could always be removed by an assembly?
questions.a: Only some texts say so; the data we have for such remote periods is incomplete and it was not an established law.

questions.q: An ancient text says a bad ruler may be removed by the assembly. A careful historian should
questions.a: note it but remember the evidence is incomplete
o: note it but remember the evidence is incomplete
treat it as a proven law

questions.q: Explain how the sabha and samiti limited the power of a raja.
questions.a: The raja was not expected to rule arbitrarily but had to take advice from assemblies of elders and ministers, and some texts say an incompetent ruler could be removed.
s: Could be removed in some texts

questions.q: Which shows a democratic feature in the ganas?
questions.a: Members of the assembly voted and selected the ruler
o: Members of the assembly voted and selected the ruler

questions.q: Compare monarchies and ganas in the way the ruler was chosen.
questions.a: In monarchies the raja was usually the son of the previous one, while in ganas the assembly members selected the ruler.

questions.q: Explain why the early republics are considered important in world history.
questions.a: They are among the earliest such systems in the world, where an assembly took decisions by discussion and vote and even chose the ruler.
s: Among the earliest in the world

questions.q: Which system, monarchy or gana, seems fairer to you? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned answer is accepted, for example gana because members shared in decisions, or monarchy for stability.

questions.q: Write a short dialogue between a raja and an elder from the sabha about a new tax.
questions.a: A dialogue where the raja proposes a tax, the elder gives advice and the raja decides with the assembly's counsel.

concepts.name: Iron, coins and other innovations
concepts.description: Schools of thought, iron metallurgy, warfare and the first coins.
concepts.idea: Iron tools and punch-marked coins changed farming, war and trade in the age of the mahajanapadas.
concepts.rule: New schools of thought (late Vedic, Buddhist, Jain) spread through travelling scholars, monks and nuns. The Harappans knew copper and bronze; in the Second Urbanisation iron metallurgy became central. Iron tools became widespread and helped agriculture on a bigger scale; iron weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze. Growing trade led to the first coins, made of silver with punched symbols, called punch-marked coins; later coins were of copper and gold.
concepts.example: A panel of the Sanchi stupa shows a smithy where workers beat the iron.

questions.q: The first Indian coins were made of ____.
questions.a: silver

questions.q: The first coins are called
questions.a: punch-marked coins

questions.q: The main new metal of the Second Urbanisation was
questions.a: iron

questions.q: Harappans were known for mastering
questions.a: copper and bronze metallurgy

questions.q: Why were coins made necessary?
questions.a: Growing trade

questions.q: Iron weapons were lighter and ____ than bronze ones.
questions.a: sharper

questions.q: Iron tools helped agriculture because they
questions.a: allowed farming on a bigger scale
o: allowed farming on a bigger scale

questions.q: What does 'punch-marked' mean?
questions.a: Symbols were punched onto a soft metal like silver
o: Symbols were punched onto a soft metal like silver
The coins were carved in stone

questions.q: State two ways iron changed life in the Second Urbanisation.
questions.a: Iron tools made large-scale farming easier and iron weapons were lighter and sharper than bronze ones.

questions.q: A farmer with an iron plough could most likely
questions.a: cultivate more land

questions.q: A trader sells goods across regions. Coins helped by
questions.a: making exchange easier

questions.q: Fill: mark each item for the First (Harappan) or the Second Urbanisation: iron, copper/bronze, Ganga plains.
questions.a: Iron and the Ganga plains belong to the Second Urbanisation; copper and bronze belong to the First.

questions.q: Why did neighbouring mahajanapadas sometimes go to war and how could iron affect it?
questions.a: Some evidence of warfare exists between neighbours, and iron made better weapons, so armies could fight more effectively.

questions.q: Why did iron take a few centuries to become part of daily life?
questions.a: Techniques were perfected first and then spread
o: Techniques were perfected first and then spread

questions.q: Explain how new ideas travelled in the age of the mahajanapadas.
questions.a: Schools of thought such as Buddhist and Jain spread through scholars, monks and nuns travelling across India and pilgrims on the roads.

questions.q: Why might a mahajanapada issue its own coins?
questions.a: To show its authority and support trade within its territory
o: To show its authority and support trade within its territory

questions.q: Compare bronze and iron for weapons.
questions.a: Iron made lighter and sharper weapons such as swords, spears, arrows and shields, while bronze was heavier and less sharp.

questions.q: Explain why iron technology and coins together supported the growth of cities.
questions.a: Iron tools raised farm output and gave weapons and tools, and coins made trade easier, so surplus, craftspeople and markets could grow in towns.

questions.q: Which was more important for urban growth, iron or coins? Give reasons.
questions.a: A reasoned choice: iron enabled farming and tools, while coins enabled trade; both supported cities.

questions.q: Design a punch-marked coin and explain the symbols you chose.
questions.a: A silver coin with punched symbols such as a tree or animal, and a note that the symbols showed the issuing region.

concepts.name: The varna-jati system
concepts.description: Groups in a complex society, jatis and varnas, the four varnas, the word caste and its flexibility and rigidity.
concepts.idea: Jatis are occupational communities and varnas are four groups from the Vedic texts; the system began flexible.
concepts.rule: A complex society organises itself into groups by class or occupation. India had a two-fold system. A jati is a group with a specific occupation, with skills passed down; jatis could divide into sub-jatis with customs of their own. The four varnas were Brahmins (knowledge and rituals), Kshatriyas (defend the land and fight), Vaishyas (trade, business, agriculture) and Shudras (artisans, workers, servants). The word caste comes from the Portuguese casta. In the early period people changed occupations when needed; the system later became rigid and led to inequality.
concepts.example: A farming community hit by drought migrated to a city and took up new work.

questions.q: A group with a specific occupation tied to livelihood is called a ____.
questions.a: jati

questions.q: How many varnas were there?
questions.a: four

questions.q: The word 'caste' comes from which language?
questions.a: Portuguese

questions.q: Which varna was expected to defend society and fight if needed?
questions.a: Kshatriyas

questions.q: Brahmins were engaged in
questions.a: preserving knowledge and performing rituals

questions.q: Vaishyas increased wealth through trade, business or ____.
questions.a: agriculture

questions.q: What is a jati?
questions.a: A community with a specific occupation whose skills pass through generations
o: A community with a specific occupation whose skills pass through generations

questions.q: In the early period, the varna-jati system was
questions.a: more flexible

questions.q: Name the four varnas and one role of each.
questions.a: Brahmins preserved knowledge and performed rituals; Kshatriyas defended and fought; Vaishyas did trade, business or farming; Shudras were artisans, craftspeople, workers or servants.

questions.q: A community of potters whose skill passes from parents to children is a
questions.a: jati

questions.q: Farmers who move to a city after a long drought and take up new work show that
questions.a: occupations could change when circumstances demanded
o: occupations could change when circumstances demanded

questions.q: Give an example from the chapter of people changing occupation and explain why it happened.
questions.a: Some Brahmins turned to trade or military activities, and drought could force farmers to take other work in cities, because circumstances demanded it.

questions.q: How can sub-jatis be different from each other?
questions.a: Each developed customs and traditions of its own, for instance about marriage, rituals or food.

questions.q: Which shows that inequality arose from social groups?
questions.a: Some groups gained more wealth, power or influence than others
o: Some groups gained more wealth, power or influence than others

questions.q: Explain why a complex society divides into groups and what problem this can bring.
questions.a: Different people concerned with governance, religion, trade, farming and crafts form groups, which helps organisation, but divisions can lead to inequalities and discrimination.

questions.q: Why did the system become rigid over time?
questions.a: It hardened with the passage of time, especially during British rule
o: It hardened with the passage of time, especially during British rule

questions.q: Compare varna and jati.
questions.a: Varna is a concept from the Vedic texts with four groups, while jati is a community with a specific occupation and many sub-groups.

questions.q: Explain the positive and the negative sides of the varna-jati system.
questions.a: It structured society and organised activities, giving stability, but as it became rigid it led to inequality and discrimination against lower jatis and excluded communities.

questions.q: Is equality desirable in a society? Give reasons.
questions.a: Yes, equality helps fairness and harmony, though societies have rarely achieved it. A reasoned answer is accepted.

questions.q: Write a short note on an initiative that reduces inequality in society.
questions.a: A note describing an initiative, such as a scholarship or an inclusive school programme, and how it reduces inequality.

concepts.name: Trade routes and cities beyond the Ganga plains
concepts.description: The Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha, Sisupalgarh, the southern kingdoms and the interconnected Subcontinent.
concepts.idea: Long-distance routes connected north and south and helped the growth of cities and kingdoms across India.
concepts.rule: Two routes were widely used: the Uttarapatha connected the northwest to the Ganga plains and eastern India, and the Dakshinapatha started from Kaushambi and crossed the Vindhya hills to the south. Ports on the coasts were centres of trade. In the east, Sisupalgarh, the capital of Kalinga, followed a strict square plan with fortifications and broad streets. In the south cities emerged from about 400 BCE and the Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas arose. The south was rich in stones, gold and spices. By 300 or 200 BCE the Subcontinent was interconnected and the mahajanapadas ceased to exist.
concepts.example: Kodumanal near Erode had shell and gemstone industries.

questions.a: Dakshinapatha

questions.a: Ganga plains and eastern India

questions.q: Which three kingdoms emerged in the south?
questions.a: Cholas, Cheras and Pandyas

questions.q: Sisupalgarh was the capital of
questions.a: Kalinga

questions.q: Why were roads important in the 1st millennium BCE?
questions.a: They served trade, pilgrimage and military campaigns
o: They served trade, pilgrimage and military campaigns

questions.q: Cities in the south began emerging from about ____ BCE.
Why did the southern regions trade profitably?
questions.a: They were rich in gems, gold and spices
o: They were rich in gems, gold and spices

questions.q: Sisupalgarh is known for
questions.a: a strict square plan with imposing fortifications
o: a strict square plan with imposing fortifications

questions.q: Describe the two main routes of the 1st millennium BCE.
questions.a: The Uttarapatha joined the northwest to eastern India through the Ganga plains, and the Dakshinapatha began at Kaushambi and crossed the Vindhya Range to the south.

questions.q: Which route would a merchant take from the northwest to eastern India?
questions.a: the Uttarapatha

questions.q: Which route crosses the Vindhya Range?
questions.a: the Dakshinapatha

questions.q: Why were coastal ports important in the 1st millennium BCE?
questions.a: They were vibrant centres of trade connected by lateral roads and linked India to kingdoms overseas.

questions.q: Why did southern kingdoms trade with the rest of India and overseas?
questions.a: They had precious and semiprecious stones, gold and spices that were in demand.

questions.q: By 300 or 200 BCE the Subcontinent was
questions.a: one vibrant interconnected land

questions.q: A merchant carries spices from the south to the Ganga plains. Suggest the route and one benefit to each region.
questions.a: He travels north along the Dakshinapatha via Kaushambi, the south earns from trade and the Ganga cities gain spices and goods.

questions.q: Why did the mahajanapadas cease to exist by about 300 BCE?
questions.a: Fresh developments and larger empires reshaped India
o: Fresh developments and larger empires reshaped India

questions.q: Compare Sisupalgarh and the early southern cities.
questions.a: Sisupalgarh in Kalinga had a strict square plan with fortifications and broad streets, while southern cities emerged from about 400 BCE with kingdoms such as Chola, Chera and Pandya.

questions.q: Explain how roads helped connect India in this period.
questions.a: Roads carried people, goods and ideas between north and south, east and west, so cultures and trade spread and India became interconnected.

questions.q: 'Trade routes were more important than armies in connecting India.' Do you agree? Justify.
questions.a: A reasoned answer such as routes connected people peacefully and spread goods and ideas, while armies created states; both mattered.

questions.q: Draw a sketch map of India showing the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha with three cities.
questions.a: A map with the Uttarapatha from the northwest to the east, the Dakshinapatha from Kaushambi to the south, and cities such as Taxila, Kaushambi and Sisupalgarh.
